title: Quasi-finiteness descends for a finitely presented affine model
statement: Let $(I,\leq)$ be a small nonempty directed partially ordered set, let $(A_i)_{i\in I}$ be a directed system of commutative rings, and let $A=\varinjlim_i A_i$ be its colimit [def-weil-pbc-category-colimit]. Fix $i_0\in I$ and a finitely presented $A_{i_0}$-algebra $B_0$ [def-weil-pbc-finitely-presented-algebra]. Put $B_i=A_i\otimes_{A_{i_0}}B_0$ for $i\geq i_0$ and $B=A\otimes_{A_{i_0}}B_0$; these tensor products of commutative algebras are the pushouts whose spectra are the affine fibre products [lem-weil-pbc-fibre-product-affine-spectra]. If $\operatorname{Spec}B\to\operatorname{Spec}A$ [def-weil-affine-spectrum] is quasi-finite [pqf-def-quasifinite], then for some $i\geq i_0$ the morphism $\operatorname{Spec}B_i\to\operatorname{Spec}A_i$ is quasi-finite.

source.place: Tag 094M, label lemma-descend-quasi-finite, specialized to affine schemes; Situation label situation-descent-property (Tag 081D).

proof.text: Restrict to the directed tail $J=\{i:i\ge i_0\}$. This does not change the ring colimit: given a cocone on the tail and $k\in I$, choose $j\ge k,i_0$ and compose $A_k\to A_j$ with its leg; directedness proves independence of $j$ and compatibility, so the universal property gives exactly a cocone on $I$. Moreover $B$ is the colimit of the $B_i$: compatible maps $B_i\to D$ are precisely a compatible family $A_i\to D$ and one map $B_0\to D$ agreeing on $A_{i_0}$, hence precisely a map from the pushout $A\otimes_{A_{i_0}}B_0$ to $D$. This proves the colimit assertion in commutative rings, including its canonical legs. Choose algebra generators $b_1,\ldots,b_n$ from a finite presentation of $B_0$. Every element of $B_i$ is a finite sum of tensors $a\otimes b$; express $b$ as a polynomial in the $b_r$, so $B_i$ is generated over $A_i$ by $1\otimes b_1,\ldots,1\otimes b_n$. Thus every $A_i\to B_i$ is of finite type.

source.place: 094M, setup of affine specialization of Situation 081D; elementary cocone and pushout argument

proof.text: By quasi-finiteness of $f:\operatorname{Spec}B\to\operatorname{Spec}A$, every point is isolated in its fibre. The scheme-fibre homeomorphism identifies these fibres with the underlying preimages, and the affine fibre-product formula identifies the fibre at a prime $\mathfrak p$ with $\operatorname{Spec}(B\otimes_A\kappa(\mathfrak p))$. Since every singleton is open, every subset is a union of open singletons, and both it and its complement are open. An irreducible closed subset cannot contain distinct points: one singleton and its complement would partition it into two proper closed subsets. Thus every nonempty irreducible closed subset is a singleton, and no strict chain of these has positive length. By the definition of Krull dimension the fibre has dimension zero if nonempty, and $-\infty$ if empty, hence at most zero in either case.

source.place: 094M: reduction to fibre dimension at most zero; 05M5 with d=0

proof.text: For $i\le j$ in the tail, the canonical map $A_j\otimes_{A_i}B_i\to B_j$ is an isomorphism: a map from either ring to $D$ is exactly maps from $A_j$ and $B_0$ to $D$ agreeing on $A_{i_0}$; equivalently, its inverse sends $a\otimes b\in B_j$ to $a\otimes(1\otimes b)$. In particular the comparison map is surjective. Apply the affine limit fibre-dimension bound to the two systems $(A_i)$ and $(B_i)$ on $J$, their ring colimits established in step 1, the finite-type maps of step 1, these surjective comparisons, and the bound of step 2 with $d=0$. It supplies $i\ge i_0$ for which every fibre $\operatorname{Spec}(B_i\otimes_{A_i}\kappa(\mathfrak p_i))$ has dimension at most zero.

Fix a prime $\mathfrak q$ of $B_i$ and let $\mathfrak p_i$ be its contraction. At its point in the fibre, the dimension at the point is at most the whole fibre dimension because the whole fibre is an open neighbourhood. It is at least zero since every neighbourhood contains that point. Hence it equals zero. The zero-fibre-dimension criterion, with the finite-type map $A_i\to B_i$ from step 1, proves quasi-finiteness at $\mathfrak q$. Using the full source and target as affine neighbourhoods in the definition of quasi-finiteness at a point proves that $f_i$ is locally quasi-finite. The morphism between these affine schemes is affine, and affine-morphism permanence makes it quasi-compact. The equivalence of quasi-finiteness with local quasi-finiteness plus quasi-compactness therefore proves that $f_i$ is quasi-finite. If $B_i$ is the zero ring there are no primes, and the same argument has a vacuous pointwise assertion.
